In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions: (1) What is the maximum link utilization level that can be achieved with a network employing the FIFO packet scheduling algorithm? (2) What is the minimum worst-case edge-to-end delay bound that can be achieved in a network employing the SETF packet scheduling algorithm? And (3) what is the minimum worstcase edge-to-end delay and the maximum link utilization that can be simultaneously achieved in a network with the DETF packet scheduling algorithm?

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, with aggregate packet scheduling algorithms, we can significantly improve the network utilization level at the cost of a higher worst-case edge-toedge delay bound.

(1) the FIFO scheduling is the most simple and least sophisticated aggregate scheduling algorithm; (2) the static earliest time-first scheduling is the most sophisticated and complex scheduling algorithm; (3) the dynamic earliest time-first is somewhere between the two extremes; (4) with additional time stamp information in the packet header, we can increase the allowable link utilization and reduce the worst-case delay bound.

, for a given network, the worst-case edge- to-edge delay bound is an increasing function of the (maximum) link utilization, and the worst-case edge-edge delay bound is a decreasing function of the sophistication of the aggregate packet scheduling algorithms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the more complex the aggregate packet scheduling algorithm is, the more network resources it can utilize and the less delay bound it can guarantee.

, for a network domain with N nodes and L links, with a (maximum) link utilization level of 0.5, we can guarantee an edge-to-edge delay no greater than N-1 time units for the FIFO algorithm, and no greater than N/2 time units for both SETF and DETF algorithms, respectively.
the more sophisticated the aggregate packet scheduling algorithm is, the more network resources can be utilized and the less the worst-case edge- to-edge delay bound is.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, for a network with a given topology, there exist a class of aggregate packet scheduling that is able to achieve an optimal link utilization level, while at the same time providing the best worst-case edge-to edge delay bound.

, in the design of aggregate packet scheduling algorithm, one should not only consider its scheduling complexity (e.g., the complexity of packet header modification) but also the additional control information (e.g., packet time stamps) that can be encoded in the packet headers to achieve the desired scheduling objective.

, with additional control information encoded in packet headers for scheduling purpose, a network can significantly increase its (maximum) allowable traffic load, and at the time reduce the worst case end-to-end delay bound.
